Now the Prime Minister
spoke with his customary vigour at Charlottetown a few weeks ago. According to the press, and that is all I have to go on, he


indicated that as a result of his Dartmouth speech, which we have all read with so much interest, the United States had made a new appraisal of its trade policies and of certain measures which had not been passed at the recent session of congress. Therefore, in the light of that optimistic forecast respecting the influence of the Canadian government in Washington we might have been pardoned for expecting great results from this Washington meeting. Well, did they occur? I think it has never been better put than by Mr. Blakely the columnist in the Montreal Gazette, when he wrote that there had been other pilgrimages to Washington-and I have taken part in them myself- which could be said to have produced nothing, but it is doubtful there have been any which could be said to have produced less than this one. The Gazette, I think although I am not sure it was on the same day, in its editorial columns, in explaining some of the difficulties that have to be faced, described this pilgrimage as a force less than irresistible which met an object not perceptibly movable.
Now with respect to the Washington communique which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance discussed at some length this afternoon, I might say I know something about communiques issued after international conferences and I have had a good deal of experience in reading between their lines. I have indeed compared this one with two other communiques previously issued after such conferences, but in this case we do not have to read between the lines. The secretary of commerce is reported to have said, which statement was explained in this house this afternoon, "We fixed them". I know it was explained by the Minister of Finance that he was speaking in a jocular way and I am sure he did not expect those words to be reproduced in the press. Perhaps that makes them all the more impressive.
The Minister of Finance referred this afternoon to the fine atmosphere of the conference and I am sure the atmosphere was fine. He said, although he did not use these words, that we really laid it on the line and made known the Canadian position exactly and in much stronger terms than previously. However, the United States undersecretary of state in charge of economic affairs, as reported in Washington, is said to have expressed some satisfaction-and perhaps the satisfaction is understandable in view of the feeling he would have had in advance of the arrival of this delegation-and to have said that the general climate on the wheat problem at these talks was better than that at the meeting he attended in Ottawa before the election. I suspect it was because at

that earlier meeting the United States government was left in no doubt as to our views and there was no desire on their part at that time to issue a communique in which we would have expressed our views.
The communique speaks for itself-the Americans will do "what they can" to help us. They will do away with these barter transactions of which my hon. friend made so much this afternoon, without emphasizing the fact that this position was taken by them before the election. It was taken, as I understand it, not in the summer as he suggests, but last April. Then the Minister of Finance explained that it was different this time in Washington. To quote from a press statement made by him on leaving that city he said:
The barter suspension has been confirmed in a Canadian context-
Whatever that may mean.
__and this places it now on a level of an international agreement beyond domestic pressures.
I would say to my hon. friend that in the light of the experience I have had in negotiating and discussing economic matters with the United States I would never have gone out on that limb. I think he probably will very soon regret his confidence.
There has been domestic pressure brought before on their congress to alter an arrangement made previously by the administration. Well, Mr. Speaker, we will see what will happen. I, like all members of this house, hope that the result will be as forecast and that the Americans will abandon these arrangements and these practices. However the most important one and perhaps the most dangerous one has not even been mentioned in the communique. That is the question of tied-in sales. In short I think we will be making a great mistake if we go overboard with optimism on the results of this conference. This talk took place-

Mr. Speaker, the rather positive speech which we have just heard reminds me of when I first entered Victoria college in 1946. I noticed a mark up on the wall and I inquired as to how it got there-it was a sort of grease stain. I was told that a number of years ago a very radical undergraduate in a moment of protest had hurled a plate of butter at the wall. I inquired as to the name of the undergraduate and what had happened to him and it was reported that he was the secretary of state for external affairs. Now the story is probably apocryphal but it is very interesting for me as a new member to sit here and watch him
The Address-Mr. Fisher spread butter in an entirely new way. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, to add my mite-spelled "mite"-to the congratulatory credits which have been accorded to you, to your deputy and to the mover (Mr. Smith, Calgary South) and the seconder (Mr. Arsenault) of the motions.
A maiden speech is usually or reportedly a moment of emotion and, at emotional times, I tend to turn to my favourite poet Sarah Binks, the prairie songstress. But not only do we have some Saskatchewan songsters here in my own party, we have a really sonorous and melodious songster on the treasury bench and so I am going to move on without any metered flourishes to the flat directness of northwestern Ontario. I plan to cover the following topics.
Firstly, the significance of the electoral result in the constituency of Port Arthur; secondly the role of the press and television in the political campaign; thirdly the problems of the constituency of Port Arthur; and fourthly, some questions on the principles and ideas of Liberals and Conservatives. That is to say the parties, not the small "1" liberal or the small "c" conservative.
Love and liking have been very noticeable in the drama which has so far unfolded in the House of Commons. Everybody loves democracy, everybody loves the monarchy, everybody loves the French language, everybody loves the old age pensioner, almost everybody loves the speech from the throne, everyone likes the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) and everyone has a great deal of respect for the Speaker.
In this sweet atmosphere I felt that I could do no less than express from a distance my appreciation of an association even in a minor way, with some of the great figures of this house.
For example, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming)-it is a conviction of mine that members of parliament do to some extent reflect the personality or the character of their constituents. A number of years ago, I earned my living in Toronto by delivering beer. Some routes in the city were much more prized than others. The member who represents Cabbagetown, or whose constituency covers that ward, may be interested to know, for example, that this area was a favourite one-one of the most prized in the city-because of the tips that were given- and one occasionally got something else as a reward for bringing the product around. One section of the city was very unpopular. That was the area of prosperity above St. Clair and centring on Eglinton. There the good women invariably insisted on a backdoor delivery, often asked that the truck be parked several doors up the way, and were very careful to give only the exact change.
336	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fisher If the hon. minister reflects such circumspect frugality, he will make an ideal minister of finance. Of course, I will watoh him closely, because we all remarked how the occasional Eglinton area housewife liked to scrub out a ketchup bottle and slip it in so as to pose as a lager bottle and reap the three cents.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to be very interested in watching the development of the party on my extreme left. I am sorry that there is to be no debate on health insurance or anything like that in the immediate future, because 1 would like to know the attitude of that party toward naturopathic medicine. I am wondering, too, whether they have any views on the McGill fence.
One last bit of personalia, Mr. Speaker, is with regard to the illustrious graduate of Victoria who is soon going to face problems in that direction. I hope the ghostly pipers of the 1948 Liberal convention will not march again, and if they do that they will not march successfully. We in this comer hope no young Lochinvar from the border comes and grabs the Liberal maiden early in 1958.
The two constituencies to the west of Port Arthur and the two constituencies to the east of Port Arthur returned Liberal members on June 10. A careless observer might say that Port Arthur's failure to do so reflected a weakness in the candidate. With all respect to the successful Liberals, such reasoning will not do. There are some reasons which I would offer for the failure of the former minister of trade and commerce to return here. I am not impudent enough to be Mr. Howe's valedictorian. The great corporations and trusts of Canada will do and are doing that chore. I would suggest, however, that our electoral victory in Port Arthur does represent a vindication for the view that the Canadian people want parliament to retain its right of free discussions, and that an abstract issue can be taken seriously by the voters. Further, the campaign in Port Arthur reveals, in my opinion, that when a C.C.F. candidate is in a fairly equal position in presenting his party's policies, a goodly portion of the electorate can appreciate its merits. One accolade one can bestow on Mr. Howe is that he never used his tremendous

power to build up a personal machine in his riding. There was no P.F.R.A. in the constituency of Port Arthur.
On this matter of party warfare and party machines I would like to refer one of the members of the treasury branch to a newsletter, No. 177, of the Canadian chamber of commerce which said:
Not very long ago a prominent provincial politician is reported to have said 'It is no secret that the country represented by the (party in power) member has a better chance of getting government help than a country where (an opposition) member is elected . . . That is only human nature, and there is nothing we can do to change that. This, in effect, tells the voters of that particular area that unless they vote the right way they can expect nothing from the government.
Recently a minister of the new government, on a lightning foray into the lakehead, made the remark that he was unaware of a certain contentious problem until the defeated Conservative candidate directed it to his notice. Gamesmanship such as this is of the spirit that the Canadian chamber of commerce deplores in its newsletter. May we have no more of it, even if in this case, Liberal members were the whipping boys.
On motion of Mr. Fisher the debate was adjourned.

Mr. Speaker, on October 15 the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) asked me certain questions pertaining to matters arising out of recent trade conferences, and I indicated at that time that I should be glad to make a statement, if it were the wish of the house, on the subject of the trade proposals and the various recent trade conferences. The following day the
hon. member pursued his question further and asked if I would include in the statement reference to the conference at Washington. Similar questions were asked by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin).
I should like to bring that statement to the house now; and as the conferences were three in number, somewhat different in character and circumstances, and all of some importance, the reports I am about to make are not as short as I should have wished they might be.	The first of these
conferences-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will my hon. friend permit an interruption? Would he not think it would be more convenient if the statement could be made under circumstances which would permit interrogations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there will be ample opportunity for the submission of questions on the statement on the orders of the day, in accordance with the practice of the house. I shall be glad to deal with them.
The first of these conferences was the conference of commonwealth finance ministers held at Mont Tremblant. That conference was proposed by the Prime Minister when he attended the conference of prime ministers at London last June. It has been the practice for the commonwealth finance ministers each year to hold a meeting following the annual meeting of the governors of the international bank and the international monetary fund at Washington. Those meetings have normally been held at Washington. On this occasion our Prime Minister proposed that the conference should be held in Canada, and that invitation was accepted.
The conference was attended by all the finance ministers of the commonwealth with the exception of New Zealand, which was represented by its minister for external affairs. The Canadian representation consisted of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), and myself, and we were supported by a very strong team of Canadian officials drawn from the departments of finance, trade and commerce and external affairs.
The preparation for the conference was intensive. It continued throughout the entire summer.

Trade Conferences
The selection of Mont Tremblant as the venue of the conference was indeed a happy one, and the circumstances there contributed very greatly to the creation of a friendly atmosphere which was conducive to understanding and to agreement.
The agenda of that conference consisted of three topics. The first concerned matters in relation to the pound sterling and problems of exchange in relation to sterling. The second topic concerned the proposed European free trade area or the European economic integration, as it is called.
These two topics were discussed at the sessions of the conference on the Saturday. On the Monday and Tuesday the conference devoted its consideration to the Canadian proposals for enlarging trade within the commonwealth and improving economic relations among the countries of the commonwealth. As hon. members are aware, the conference achieved agreement, and the extent of the agreement and the enthusiasm with which that agreement was hailed by the ministerial representatives of the commonwealth countries are alike testimony to the success of the conference. It is a pleasure indeed to assure the house that as the result of the unanimous decision that was taken at that Mont Tremblant conference, a full dress commonwealth trade and economic conference will be held some time next year. The place has not been finally decided. The date has not been finally decided. The Canadian government has extended to the governments of the other countries of the commonwealth an invitation to hold the conference in Canada. In due course we expect a final answer to that invitation.
I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that a great deal of preparation, as was recognized by the ministers of finance, will be required for such a conference, and plans have been made and are proceeding for a conference of officials, drawn from the various countries, to be held at a time and place yet to be agreed upon. The officials will have the responsibility at such a meeting for shaping the agenda for the conference and arranging plans.
I wish, in concluding my remarks on the Mont Tremblant conference, to say that in the closing meeting of the conference, which was public, minister after minister testified to his belief that the conference had achieved significant results and had done something worthy in strengthening commonwealth consciousness and fellow feeling. By leave of the house, Mr. Speaker, I now table the communique that was issued at the close of the conference by the ministers there present.

speechtext:
I turn now to the second
subject, which concerns bilateral discussions between Canada and the United Kingdom. Prior to the Mont Tremblant conference we had received information from the Chancellor of the Exchequer that it was the wish of the United Kingdom ministers who were attending the conference to come to Ottawa at the conclusion of the Mont Tremblant conference for a discussion of matters of mutual interest. We had no indication of the particular matters they proposed to discuss with us when that suggestion was made to us. We, of course, said the Canadian ministers concerned would be more than pleased to make themselves available to meet with their counterparts in the British government in any discussions. I stress the fact that there was no indication of an agenda, and that there was no suggestion of a formal conference. I think that fact needs to be clearly understood.
On the Saturday, during the progress of the first day's sittings of the Mont Tremblant conference, a news story appeared in the Montreal Daily Star, and copies of that newspaper became available during the afternoon recess at Mont Tremblant. That news story purported to refer to the intention of the United Kingdom ministers to propose the establishment of a free trade area between the United Kingdom and Canada. I had been designated by the conference as its chairman and also as the individual to give to the press each day statements on such matters as were discussed at the conference. The house will realize, of course, that the proceedings of the conference were closed.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Secret.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext:
A meeting was arranged with the press that evening for that purpose. In the course of the meeting questions were asked concerning the proposal that had been reported in the news report to which I have just referred. The Chancellor of the Exchequer and I were both present and took part in the conference. In reply to those questions the Chancellor of the Exchequer outlined a proposal which he indicated he intended to submit to the Canadian government when he came on to Ottawa the following week at the conclusion of the Mont Tremblant conference. It was a proposal, as he indicated in reply to various questions, for the establishment of a free trade area between the two countries, and to achieve it on a progressive basis over a period of years.

It was obviously a very far-reaching proposal. In the course of that conference I was invited to state the attitude of the Canadian government with respect to that proposal. Obviously it would have been improper of me to do such a thing under the circumstances. The proposal had not yet been submitted. Obviously it had never been before the Canadian government. I was just listening in the course of Mr. Thorneycroft's answers to the questions put to him at the conference as to the features of the proposal as he unfolded them at that time, and I declined- and I think quite properly so-to make any comment on that proposal except to say that I thought it would be realized that it would involve formidable difficulties in any consideration that might be given to it by the Canadian government. However, until the proposal had been set forth and submitted, I indicated that I could not undertake to make any comments on it.
That, Mr. Speaker, was the end of that matter so far as the Mont Tremblant conference was concerned. That matter was never discussed at the Mont Tremblant conference. It never had any place whatever in the proceedings of the conference. Indeed, it would not have been permissible to introduce it. In that conference we were engaged in a discussion of commonwealth trade and the Canadian proposal for the holding of a commonwealth trade and economic conference. I may say to the house that no bilateral arrangements were discussed in the course of the conference proceedings.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that what I have said will leave no room for doubt, and that there will be an end to such confusion as has been evidenced on this subject.
At the conclusion of the Mont Tremblant conference two of the British ministers, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Thorney-croft, and the president of the board of trade, Sir David Eccles, came on to Ottawa. In the course of two or three days of meetings here the United Kingdom ministers submitted a proposal in relation to the establishment of a free trade area between Canada and the United Kingdom to be brought about over a period which, we were told, might be in the neighbourhood of, say, 12 to 15 years.
I wish here to say one word by way of clarification of a matter which has been referred to more than once in this connection. That is the matter which the Prime Minister mentioned on his return to Ottawa from the conference of prime ministers last summer, when at the airport he pointed out in reply to questions put to him that the diversion from the United States to the United Kingdom of 15 per cent of the purchases which

Canadians are now making in the United States would redress a trade situation which I think must and does give a great many Canadians serious concern.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I recognize that this is one of those difficult problems with which Your Honour will have to deal, namely the latitude to be allowed to ministers in making statements on the order for motions. You will find in the records of this house plenty of discussions on this point in which my hon. friends opposite have taken part. It does seem to me that the house is willing to accept the practice that ministers be permitted, either on motions or on orders of the day, to make announcements, statements of ministerial changes or explanations of government policy having the character of an announcement or being of an urgent nature. This is shown by the fact that the house was generous today in not objecting to what the Minister of Finance asked for at the start. But with all respect it does seem to me he is now really indulging in debate. He has not announced anything new. He has commented on things that have been said about statements made by the Prime Minister and, with respect, I think Your Honour should consider whether this is the time to make a statement like this.
I am not quarrelling very much as to the difference between making statements on motions and on orders of the day. That difference is not great. If a statement is made on motions we can ask questions on orders of the day, but I think it has been ruled in the past that it is better to make such statements on orders of the day so that members can ask questions right away. It is not an announcement of government policy; it is a matter of debate, and I think the minister should have waited his turn to take part in the debate on the address. I appreciate what hon. members have drawn to my attention, and perhaps I shpuld say a word before any further steps are taken along this course. Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should make any comment except to say that there are many precedents which can be pointed out, and that I had prepared the statement at the request of the hon. member for Essex East.
Mr. Speaker, I was mentioning the background of the matters discussed in the informal discussions here in Ottawa. The basis of

what the Prime Minister said on the occasion I mentioned, having regard to the deficit in our trade with the United States, was to seek a diversion from the United States to the United Kingdom of purchases that Canada is now making from the United States. It was not part of that proposal to divert to the United Kingdom purchases by Canadians of Canadian products. The proposal of the United Kingdom ministers therefore introduced quite a new dimension into the considerations which had arisen out of the Prime Minister's reference.
In these several days of discussion here in Ottawa many matters pertaining to the trade interests of the two countries were discussed. The proceedings were very informal in character; the discussions were frank and friendly. The discussions were necessarily of a preliminary character because, for instance, the United Kingdom ministers were not authorized to discuss the question of imports of Canadian agricultural products into the United Kingdom.
It was agreed in the light of the discussion, and of the circumstances, that it was important to achieve the holding of the commonwealth trade conference next year, and as the proposal of the United Kingdom was of a long-range nature, which neither required nor was expected to be given immediate consideration by the Canadian government, or even consideration prior to the commonwealth trade and economic conference, that the matter should rest there in the form in which it was referred to later in the communique which was issued.
As to the proposals advanced by the Canadian government, I mention this only briefly to indicate that we propose to seek, wherever possible, to transfer government purchases that are now being made in the United States to the United Kingdom on terms that are fair to all concerned; to enlarge as soon as may be the amounts of goods purchased that tourists may bring back with them following visits to the United Kingdom.
Then in the third place-and this, in the view of the government, is one of very considerable importance, sir-we propose to send to the United Kingdom next month the most important trade mission which Canada has ever sent abroad. It will be a large trade mission; it will be a mission sponsored by the Canadian government, and it will include leading representatives of business, industry, labour, agriculture and other primary production from all areas of Canada.
In leaving that subject, sir, may I table the communique or agreed statement that

speechtext:
The third of the conferences, Mr. Speaker, was held at Washington. It was the third meeting of the joint United States-Canadian committee on trade and economic matters. The first two meetings of that committee had been held in March, 1954, and September, 1955, respectively. This, therefore, was the first meeting of that committee in more than two years; and, having regard to the fact that there had been a change of government in Canada, it was particularly opportune that the meeting should then be held.
The Canadian ministers who were members of the committee went to Washington then at the invitation of the United States government. The committee has definite limits set upon the scope of its consideration. Its terms of reference are limited, sir. They are, first, to consider matters affecting the harmonious economic relations between the two countries; second, in particular, to exchange information and views on matters which might adversely affect the high level of mutually profitable trade which has been built up; third, to report to the respective governments on such discussions in order that consideration may be given to measures deemed appropriate and necessary to improve economic relations and to encourage the flow of trade. The purpose of the conference, therefore, broadly speaking was an exchange of points of view.
The committee has no power of its own to arrive at definite conclusions.
The purpose of the Canadian delegation, which consisted of four ministers, my colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) and myself, assisted by a very strong team of officials from the four departments concerned, was to place before the four members of the United States cabinet the point of view that we considered to be a true representation of the feeling of the Canadian people concerning the trend of trade between the two countries, and the effect upon the well-being of Canadian agriculture of the policies being followed by the United States administration in the disposal of agricultural surpluses.
The proceedings were informal, intimate, frank and friendly. The discussions were
Trade Conferences
characterized by a vigorous presentation of the points of view of both governments, and I may say that so far as the presentation of the Canadian point of view was concerned it was put forward just as vigorously as it has been put forward at any time by the persons concerned on the floor of this House of Commons.
Now, sir, the proceedings continued for two days. As to the results of the conference,
I think briefly they can be put under four headings. First, I think there was value in the conference in that it afforded an opportunity for a frank exchange of points of view; second, it afforded an opportunity for the exchange of information, and in that exchange I think representatives of both countries derived information that will be of benefit to them in shaping their policies in certain respects. Third-perhaps this may not be so important-it afforded an opportunity for the ministers of both countries to become acquainted with their opposite numbers; and fourth-and perhaps of most direct interest- was the decision that was arrived at in reference to one particular feature of the methods pursued by the United States administration in the disposal of agricultural surpluses. We received from the four United States secretaries an affirmation in these terms:
The United States members affirm to the Canadian ministers their intention in all surplus disposal activities to avoid, in so far as possible, interfering with normal commercial marketings.
They gave assurance that under the present revised commodity credit corporation barter program each barter contract must result in a net increase in exports of the agricultural commodity involved, and that interest must be paid until the strategic materials are delivered or payment is otherwise effected for the agricultural commodities.
The United States administration, through the secretary for agriculture, had made a somewhat similar statement about the middle of the summer in regard to the barter feature of the methods pursued by the United States administration in disposing of agricultural surpluses. This is the first time to our knowledge that this has become a matter of undertaking on the part of the United States administration to any other government. While we would like to have seen some assurances that all the objectionable features in the methods pursued by the United States administration-that is, objectionable from the Canadian point of view-in their agricultural disposal program would be eliminated, at any rate this was an assurance that, so far as it went, we were glad to receive.
Now, sir, I think I should ask the leave of the house to table the communique that was agreed upon at the conference and was

Trade Conferences
issued on October 8, embodying the conclusions and reviewing the nature of the discussions on various topics carried on at that conference.
I make just this one observation in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. While the realm of positive agreement resulting from the Washington meetings is necessarily limited, limited by the nature of the meeting and limited by the powers of the committee, it was felt by the Canadian ministers who attended that conference that the conference had served a very useful purpose.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure you at once that I am not going to overlook your warning that this could not be the occasion for a debate. Hon. members on both sides will have their own views as to how near or how close to a debate on the subject the Minister of Finance chose to tread. The conferences in question have all had to do very much with all the external trade policies of the Canadian government, and certainly cannot be dealt with in the limits that are indicated in the warning you gave when a point of order was submitted to you a few moments ago.
There will certainly be other opportunities, because there are very diverging views as to the achievements the hon. gentleman has mentioned in the statement he made today. The substance, I think, is summarized as glamorously as it could be made to appear in the communiques which have been laid on the table and which we have all had the opportunity of reading in the press before this day. The views that have been expressed about the limited extent of those achievements are not apt to be very much affected by the statement we have just heard from the Minister of Finance.
It may very well be that there will be some questions on the orders of the day or at another more opportune moment to elucidate some of the points touched upon by the Minister of Finance in his statement, and there is no doubt that, Canada being in proportion to its population perhaps the most active trading nation in the world, there should be all sorts of complications resulting from the channels trade takes in the interests of those who are engaged in that trade.
It may be that the hon. gentlemen feel that the methods that were resorted to by the previous government can be pursued with greater vigour by them than they were by their predecessors, but that also is a matter about which there are very serious diverging views. The only new suggestion that seems to have arisen with respect to this attempt to divert trade, not from Canadian

production but from United States sources to United Kingdom sources, is the increase in the allowance that tourists may have for purchases made in the United Kingdom on the occasion of a trip to that country. That would not have any substantial effect in diverting trade from United States sources to British sources and would perhaps have some effect, although not serious, upon a possible diversion of some trade from Canadian production to the producers of the country the tourists would have visited.
These are all matters that deserve very careful consideration, and about which more will be required than the statement just made by the Minister of Finance to destroy the impression that nothing very new has transpired.

The first time the Canadian government received that proposal, as a proposal with any aspect of definiteness to it at all, was when on returning from Mont Tremblant and arriving in Ottawa I received a written communication from the Chancellor of the Exchequer embodying the proposal; that was the first time. The hon. member asks about the visit of the British Minister of Food and Agriculture, Right Hon. Derick Heathcoat-Amory. When Mr. Amory was here in the course of a tour across Canada he touched very lightly on the possibility that the United Kingdom ministers, when they came here later on, might be putting forward some suggestion of a free trade area. But he did not put forward any proposal, on behalf of his government, as a proposal to the Canadian government. Let me make that very clear.
What was next in this group of questions? Oh, yes; the hon. member referred to some trip that Sir David Eccles is supposed to have made to this country.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: No, the trip Sir David Eccles made from Washington to visit the Prime Minister when he was at the United Nations.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says that is not true. I think that is plain. Sir David Eccles was one of the British ministers attending the Mont Tremblant conference with the Chancellor of the Exchequer. He came to Ottawa for the several days of discussion. There was a third member of the British cabinet, Right Hon. Reginald Maudling, the paymaster general, who attended the Mont Tremblant conference but who did not come on to Ottawa.
The next question the hon. member asked was whether this had not been discussed in Washington. The hon. member shakes his head, so may I get the question right?

speechtext:
The question I asked about Washington was whether or not my hon. friend discussed the proposal made to the press gallery by the Prime Minister of

Canada, that there should be a diversion of Canadian purchases from the United States to the United Kingdom. The report is that the Minister of Finance said that that proposal was a long-term one, and the impression was created from reading the particular article that the Minister of Finance did not believe the proposal by the Prime Minister of Canada was to be taken too seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East has got his facts all wrong, as usual. Let me say this. There was nothing said by the Minister of Finance to the press at Washington or elsewhere to indicate or suggest that what the Prime Minister of Canada had said about a diversion of trade from the United States to the United Kingdom was not to be taken seriously. On the contrary, what the Minister of Finance said on all such occasions was that obviously this is something that cannot be accomplished overnight. It never was suggested it could be accomplished overnight, but it was put forward by the Prime Minister as an objective and it remains an objective of the Canadian government. If the hon. member wants the reasons I can give them to him.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Do it on a proper occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Oh, I see. It is all right for the questions to be asked with all the insinuations in them, but the questions are not to be answered when it does not suit the purposes of hon. gentlemen opposite. It is the same old closure complex.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: You have no respect for any of the rules of the house.

the Chancellor of the Exchequer was a secret communication and is privileged. The hon. member should not attempt to try to give anybody the impression that this is a departure from the position that he and his colleagues took day in and day out in the house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Is it true that following on his visit to Washington he was "fixed"? Is it equally true that after the British proposal on free trade he was transfixed?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer to both questions is no. In order that the record may be fair on this point I think I should say that, when I was in Washington, I heard about this remark that was attributed to Mr. Weeks, the remark being "We fixed 'em". I realized at once that it was purely a jocular remark-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext:
because it had no validity as applied to anything that happened in the conference. Naturally, under the circumstances, I was a little disappointed to find that some newspapers not friendly to the new government took this comment up and tried to make much of it. I therefore communicated with Mr. Weeks about it, realizing that this use that was being made of a chance jocular remark did not do him justice. Mr. Weeks issued, from the United States embassy here in Ottawa several days ago, the following statement:
I was deeply concerned to learn that the meaning of a chance colloquialism of mine is being misrepresented to give a false impression of the fine accomplishments and excellent team work resulting from the recent conferences between representatives of Canada and the United States.
As I left one of the meetings I was asked for comments and in a hurried jest without even pausing for discussion I responded, "We fixed 'em" -obviously meaning only that we, all of us, Canadians and Americans together, had fixed or settled a lot of things. The fact is that never have I said or implied or felt that the meeting was other than a great success from the standpoint of our mutual objectives. This year's meeting was the third in which I have sat and one of the best of the whole series.
No peoples are more closely bound by friendship and respect than are Canadians and Americans. The grave problems of this age are compelling reasons for greater mutual understanding and cooperation.
It is this spirit of respect and friendship and not distorted chance remarks that reveal my appreciation of the representatives of Canada and their

great independent nation. Such esteem, I assure you, is shared by all Americans associated in the recent conference.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance with regard to the recent discussions in Washington. Was the minister made aware of the tie-in or tie-up between the metal crisis at this time and the disposal program of the United States government? This is a matter of a good deal of interest at this time because of the crisis existing in metals in Canada at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that matter was discussed. It was a matter of considerable concern to the Canadian government, and we were extremely anxious to know what were the plans of the United States government both with regard to the possibility of continued stockpiling and also with reference to the possibility of tariff action against Canadian metals, in particular zinc and lead. This matter was fully discussed, and in the communique the hon. member will find reference to the subject.
So far as the first matter is concerned, namely the policy on stockpiling, I may tell him that the United States government is not continuing the policy of stockpiling of these particular metals which Canada has been exporting in quantity to the United States. So far as the possibility of future United States tariff action against Canadian lead and zinc is concerned, the communique contains the following:
The Canadian ministers expressed concern over the effect on Canadian producers which would result from any future action by the United States to raise duties on imported lead and zinc. The United States members explained the situation confronting their domestic producers. They called attention to the continued need for imports of certain minerals and metals and indicated that any United States tariff action that might be taken to relieve serious injury to United States producers would have the primary objective of maintaining a normal relationship between imports and domestic production. They noted that any such action would be applied in accordance with the procedures of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
I am sure the hon. member is aware that the United States tariff rates on importations of lead and zinc-and this applies to imports

Trade Conferences
of these two base metals from Canada-are bound by the general agreement on tariffs and trade. If the United States congress at the next session proceeds to increase tariffs on imports of lead and zinc so far as Canada is concerned, it will mean that the United States will have to obtain, from the countries which are signatories to GATT, agreement to waive the provisions in that respect. That will give the countries concerned the right, if they so choose, to demand concessions.
In conclusion I may assure the hon. gentleman that the Canadian government regards this as a matter of serious concern, and pressed the case of the Canadian producers of zinc and lead very firmly and very hard.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Pressed it how?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON RECENT CONFERENCES
speechtext: Yes, we pressed the case for the Canadian producers of all metals. There was extensive discussion on the subject.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Is the minister aware that when a farmer makes application for a loan from the Canadian farm loan board the board, before acknowledging the request, informs implement companies in the area of the application and of the board's disposition of the request for the loan? If the minister finds this to be the case, will he assure the house that he will instruct the board to cease immediately this unethical, high-handed and deplorable practice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORTED DISCLOSURES OF INFORMATION RESPECTING LOAN APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member telephoned me fifteen minutes before the session opened this afternoon to inform me that he was aware of a case in which, while an application by a farmer to the Canadian farm loan board was pending and the farmer had not yet been notified as to the disposition of the case, an implement firm to which he was indebted was notified by the board that the board was declining the application. I expressed some surprise at that. I can assure the hon. member, and I can assure the house, that if the board has done what he intimates, it will not do it again.
As I understand it, an application by a farmer to the loan board is not a public matter and it is certainly not a matter to be discussed with persons who may be interested in the affairs of an applicant farmer.
Inquiries of the Ministry I have asked the hon. member to give me particulars of the case in question. I can assure the house that I will make it my business to go to the bottom of this matter; and if this sort of thing is happening I can assure him that as far as I am concerned I shall see to it that it has happened for the last time.

subtopic: FERRY "WILLIAM CARSON"

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: FERRY "WILLIAM CARSON"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. When will the minister carry out the recommendation by the Newfoundland board of trade for the ferry William Carson to carry passengers on her run between Argentia and North Sydney?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: FERRY "WILLIAM CARSON"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of this question. The question of the M.V. William Carson carrying passengers and automobiles in addition to freight on its temporary run between North Sydney and Argentia has been before the management of the Canadian National Railways and the former minister of transport on several occasions in the past. In announcing the service the former minister spoke in the house on July 20, 1955, as follows:
In the meantime the William Carson will, within the next few weeks, be placed in service by the C.N.R. on a limited basis between North Sydney and Argentia. Because the ship is designed to fit into specialized unloading and loading facilities that are available only at North Sydney and Port aux Basques, this temporary service to Argentia will be for freight movement only and will not provide for passengers or the carrying of automobiles. This temporary service to Argentia will provide valuable experience as to the operation of this highly specialized ship and should bring about an improvement in the carriage of freight to and from Newfoundland.
Since then, as I say, the matter of carrying passengers and automobiles was considered from time to time but no action was taken. I am advised that the William Carson is a highly specialized vessel in many respects, and in particular the ship requires special shore facilities in order to function properly; and that to accommodate passengers and automobiles on the run to Argentia would mean a substantial expansion of facilities.
I discussed this matter with the Newfoundland board of trade when 1 was in St. John's a month or two ago, and they told me that in their opinion automobiles could be landed and taken off this vessel at Argentia. I asked

Inquiries of the Ministry them if they had actually seen it done, or taken cars on and off the vessel, and they said they had not. I said: if you can go down to Argentia and demonstrate to the officials of the C.N.R. that cars can be moved on and off that vessel without danger I will recommend to the C.N.R. that cars should be loaded. I have not heard from the Newfoundland board of trade on the matter since that time.

Mr. Speaker, this being a matter which comes under the Department of Agriculture the Prime Minister has referred it to me. The answer is as follows: FAO proposed a world food board at Copenhagen in 1946. In subsequent months the proposal was reviewed in Washington by a special international commission. The commission, in which Canada was represented, recommended against the formation of such a body. This was subsequently followed by several other proposals, one for the establishment of an international commodity clearing house. None of these has met with acceptance by the member nations of FAO.
FAO then established its committee on commodity problems to review commodity situations and to consider surpluses. This was followed by the establishment of a special subcommittee in Washington which meets frequently to review surplus problems and to provide a forum for discussion. The committee prepared a set of principles relating to surplus disposal, designed among other things to eliminate or reduce competition with commercial transactions when surpluses are disposed of on concessional terms. Some 30 countries, including the leading trading nations, have subscribed to these principles. speechtext:
Shortly before the adjournment last night, I had been advocating an extension of trade with the sterling area, the acceptance of inconvertible currency and the spending of that sterling to buy goods in the sterling area that we are presently buying from the United States. In that way we would enable the sterling area to achieve a greater degree of balance with Canada, and would enable Canada to achieve a greater degree of balance with the United States, or at least to reduce our imbalance of trade with that country.
96698-21i
The Address-Mr. Quelch
My time is limited, but I wish to say a few words regarding the surplus disposal program of the United States. The former government was very critical of that program, and I gather the present government is not very much more favourably disposed towards it. I feel the United States is to be highly commended upon that program because under it the United States today is making surplus food available to the hungry people of nations that are not able to obtain food through the normal channels of trade. At the same time the United States is paying the farmers a fair price for that food.
Let me state very briefly the history of this surplus. It will be recalled that in the latter years of the war the food and agricultural organization warned the nations of the world that two-thirds of the population of the world was hungry. They further warned that unless the nations that had the ability to expand the production of their food did everything in their power to do so there may be worldwide starvation. The United States went all out to expand production of food. They paid very substantial support prices to their farmers, and as a consequence the United States did build up a substantial reserve of food in the form of farm products.
Unfortunately the food and agricultural organization did not provide the international machinery to distribute this surplus to the nations that needed it. It is true that they did bring forth a proposal for a world food bank but that was rejected by member nations. Then, I think it was in 1950, they proposed an international commodity clearing house. Personally, I felt that was an excellent idea, but again the member nations rejected it. So, we found we had a situation where the surpluses of each country were left on their own doorsteps.
It was then that the United States expanded the program by which they would be able to distribute surplus food to the nations that needed it. They proclaimed, in effect, that any nation that was not able to obtain the food they needed through the normal channels of trade would be able to obtain their food from the United States, if the United States had it in surplus quantity, by the acceptance of their currency, by barter agreement or, in a case of dire distress, by outright gift. Let me point out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that the United States did not wait for some nation to ask them to accept their currency. They saw the problem and they believed the solution to that problem was to accept foreign currency. As a result of that the United States has sold hundreds of millions of dollars worth of food for foreign currency. I am

The Address-Mr. Macdonnell not suggesting for one minute that we should go as far as the United States did, but I am suggesting we could go as far as I have suggested. We could accept inconvertible sterling for the goods we export to the sterling area, and then spend that inconvertible sterling in the sterling area to buy the goods which we are at present buying from the United States.
In that way we might accomplish the proclaimed purpose of the Prime Minister. I can recall that some years ago, the Prime Minister supported a motion to accept sterling. I am therefore hopeful that he will regard that proposal in a sympathetic way. I believe the proposal I put forward is the logical way in which to achieve the Prime Minister's objective of diverting 15 per cent of our imports from the United States to the sterling area.
I listened to the long statement of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. After we have read that statement we shall have an opportunity to sift the wheat from the chaff, if we can find any. But I must say that on the face of it that statement does not seem to provide much hope for any considerable increase in trade. I say that for the reason that it does not provide for any substantial change in policy.

Indeed, I remember suggesting to them once that they might follow the prayer of the highland minister who said to his flock: "Oh Lord, if it be possible, make us worthy in some measure of the high esteem in which we hold ourselves". I hope that the then ministers took cognizance of what I said.
But the other thing that struck us sitting opposite them in those days was that the high esteem brought with it also a feeling of indispensability. It is surprising that even with the most modest men, when they have power for more than a certain amount of time I think a feeling of indispensability creeps over them. I had an illustration of it once some years ago when we in the opposition had won several by-elections. I had a very pleasant letter from a member of the government who congratulated me on the victory but who said, "Of course it could not happen in a general election, could it?"
I think that was the attitude that crept over members of the government. They felt that, among other things, we were not competent, that we could not form a government. I think the Canadian people felt differently and have demonstrated differently. But when the election came I think it was hardly dreamt of in their philosophy that anyone could take their place. I might describe their feeling I think as the feeling that the change could hardly have happened. I might describe it by the answer of the little boy who had learned his twelve times twelve tables and who when asked thirteen times two said "You can't". I feel that in the same way the members of the government, after being defeated on June 10, really felt "You can't".
After the Prime Minister's speech which was mild and, I felt, almost apologetic, I was reminded of Benjamin Disraeli's description of the treasury bench sitting opposite to him so many years ago. Here are his words describing the Liberal treasury bench sitting opposite:
Some took refuge in melancholy, and their eminent chief alternated between a menace and a sigh. As I sat opposite the treasury bench, the ministers reminded me of one of those marine

landscapes not very unusual on the coasts of South America. You behold a range of exhausted volcanoes. Not a flame flickers on a single pallid crest. But the situation is still dangerous. There are occasional earthquakes and ever and anon the dark rumbling of the sea.
It is true that since then there have not been what I would call earthquakes, I would rather call them small tremors like the small outbursts from the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) and the milder one from the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Marler). But in general the attitude of the opposition has been conciliatory.
As for the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the former minister of health and welfare, it is interesting to see him in the opposition. We remember his technique in the government. We remember how. in answering questions, he would give more or less of an answer; he would use words having some vague relation to the question and then the desk would open and a prepared speech would be produced in which we had eloquent testimony to the excellence of the government. The question was just a peg on which to hang it. It was a well developed technique. Then the minister, as I said, would soar away, using the question as a springboard.
But I think the greatest surprise was the former minister of agriculture. Instead of a lion we had a lamb or, perhaps better, a dove of peace bearing olive branches. The only thing that seemed to be the same was the glass of water. The minister is fortunate because no one will doubt that it was a glass of water. No one will suspect that he did what Disraeli is reported to have done in one of his several-hour speeches. He was drinking frequently of a white liquid and it is said that the liquid was not water at all but gin and that he consumed two bottles of it during his speech. I admit that the speech was several hours long. No one will suspect the former minister of agriculture of doing that.
I was touched by the height of patriotic devotion he showed in explaining the attitude of the party. He claimed that it was in effect "high and lifted up", that it was going to concern itself only with the welfare of the country and not with any party advantage. He admonished the other parties in the house that they should do the same thing.
If the minister will allow me to do so, I should like to put in a little plug for him by relating a remark which I understand he made when he was first in this house. I have quoted it previously and I hope he will not

I believe and I am happy to believe that the new government has introduced a new spirit. I believe that the Prime Minister has taken, virtually from the dust-bin, ideas in which the previous government were not interested, and he has made people think and talk about them in a way that they have not done for years.
I think we can say that instead of gloom and hesitation, we now have action and hope. The trade difficulties with Britain and the United States are fully recognized but they have been grappled with. This has been recognized both at home and abroad. The Financial Times of London, in speaking of the commonwealth conference in London, referred to it as unusually successful and they gave credit to the present Prime Minister. I have already mentioned the statement that co-operation in the past was handicapped by Canadian indifference. Now on July 8 the Financial Times of London, referring to the commonwealth economic conference as a desirable achievement, said that the Prime Minister has "shaken up the settled and defeatist thinking which had already abandoned hope of the expansion of commonwealth trade". Those are their words and I believe them to be true, in fact they so exactly express my own feelings that I wish I had written them myself.
This I think describes well what has been done. If the spirit is right impossible things can be accomplished. I remember the music hall catch phrase, "where there is a will there are three ways". Well, I think there has not been a will and while difficulties remain and we do not have any magic wand with which to brush them off, nevertheless there is a new spirit.
The Montreal Gazette stressed the importance of the conference and mentions very properly the anxiety that Britain might move more and more into the European trade orbit. This is an appealing reason for vigorous

action and for this reason, to quote again the Gazette, "the Prime Minister's proposal comes just at the moment when the needs and opportunities of commonwealth trade ought to be put forward."
Let us now turn to the United States. There are problems there which we all know exist and there again the Prime Minister has spoken and his remarks on the American situation and the general attitude he has expressed have been seriously and favourably received by the American press. The Washington Post refers to the Prime Minister's frank yet friendly remarks and goes on to say that "the traditional friendship of the two countries can only be preserved and fostered by such straightforward exchange of views." This speech of the Prime Minister incidentally was carried over the C.B.S. national network and the New York Times refers to it as "a sobering indictment coming from one who is clearly a champion of Canadian-United States unity." Further on, referring to the Prime Minister's "spirit of candor" and willingness to seek mutually satisfactory solutions, it said these provide a setting for ironing out the present irritants.
We are not content with words; action is not lacking. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has been to Europe and is organizing an imposing delegation of well-known businessmen to go there again soon. I think it is fair to say that what vigour, courage and imagination can accomplish has been and will be done.
It is true that time has been lost. The last government was content to ride the crest of the wave and even now there is evidence that the former government does not know the score. The former minister of finance in a speech the other day complained that the new government was upsetting "normal and healthy trade lanes". I wonder if he has heard of the imbalance of trade? I wonder if he has heard of the danger of higher tariffs and all the other difficulties which confront us? I wonder if, in the light of that, he is complaining that there is a vigorous and sincere attempt being made to marshal the countries in the commonwealth to deal with them, an effort which has been set on foot by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and in which he is so ably seconded by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

He referred to price controls during the last war and spoke of the
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell kind of public planning that was used then and seemed willing to return to it. I wonder how far the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is ready to go. I am going to read to the house for a few moments a few sentences describing what controls were like before they were abolished. Here is a brief picture of controls as they existed at the end of the war: First, we have the chairman, the deputy chairman and members of the board. Then we have what are called the head office divisions, of which there are twelve, each with a supervisor or secretary or controller, as the case may be. Then we come to what are called the associated companies, of which there are several. Then we go on to what are called co-ordinations. These include capital equipment, foods, pulp and paper, textiles and clothing, and emergency shelter. Then we go on to a directory of administrations, and here we really plunge into big things, because on a short count I find that the directory of administrations includes about 150. I should like to direct your attention to just a few of them. There is one for books and writing paper; for cork and cork products; for fertilizers and pesticides; clothing and woollens; honey. There is jewellery, which is divided into seven categories. There is meat and meat products; there is fruit. There is one category which I find very interesting: cleaning, decorating, hairdressing, painting, renovating, undertaking, warehousing and storage.
Is this really what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar wants? May I remind him that the British labour party has been steering away from controls for some years. Several years ago at their annual meeting there was a striking vote against nationalization. At their recent meeting their policy with regard to nationalization was watered down to the following further extent:
"Labour will reserve the right to extend public ownership in any industry or part of industry which, after thorough investigation, is found to be seriously failing the nation. This will not necessarily mean taking over the entire industry; it may be that the solution will lie in the acquisition for the community of one or a number of firms."
In other words, this is a striking illustration of the way in which United Kingdom labour policy is turning away from nationalization. And this is indicated particularly by its new policy to allow the proposed national pension fund to invest in equities provided these acquisitions are to be guided solely by investment considerations and will not be aimed at securing control.

All that there is of worth, of greatness, of generosity in that device, we have today in Canada:	that is our conquest. We have liberty,
absolute, complete, . . . liberty for our religion, with its worship, its ceremonies, its prayers, its customs: liberty for our language, which is the official language as English is. Equality is ours; fraternity is ours. There is with us no domination of one race over another . . .
I suggest to the hon. member for Laurier that he might have been better employed in bringing this to our attention rather than in seeking, seeking, seeking for past events on which to base suggestions of discord.
I wish to say this. I believe that the present Leader of the Opposition-I got it right that time-so far as he was personally concerned was completely in the Laurier tradition and I hope the hon. member for Laurier may perhaps from here on follow the Laurier tradition.

What I have been trying to say in my poor French is this: I hope and believe those who have served with me in this house will agree that I have sincerely desired racial understanding and good will. The day before yesterday the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) eloquently expressed my views. Surely racial feeling between the two original races should be put away once and for all. We of the two old races have shared joys and sorrows in peace and war and I believe that our party, now that it is in power, will give such a lead that we may look confidently to closer and closer racial sympathy and understanding.
It is four months since the election. What is the record? Speaking with, I believe, some detachment, because I have not the burden of a department, I can say that never in my experience have men worked harder. Paraphrasing Sir Winston Churchill, I might say never was more work done by so few in so short a time. They have worked desperately hard.
Now as to quality. If we judge by one of the great acid tests, the answering of questions in this house,-and bear in mind that they had only a few months to master situations which some of the questioners had been familiar with for years-my feeling, with whatever detachment I am capable of, is that we in this party have everything to be proud of and nothing to be ashamed of in what they have done. I believe the people of Canada will so regard us. Legislation has come forward and will come forward rapidly, giving complete evidence of the implementing of promises which were made. The Prime Minister has made a distinct impression on the economic thinking of the United States and of the commonwealth and has paved the way, not for magic solution, but for patient and enduring struggle with the problems which exist between us and the United States on the one side and between us and the commonwealth on the other. I believe that when the people of Canada survey what has been done if we are able to carry on as we have done, as I believe we surely shall, when the time comes for another election there will be no doubt as to the result and we shall come back with a complete and over-all majority.

I admit, of course, as we all admit -the hon. member who just sat down referred to it-that they inherited problems, many serious problems; problems that faced us in June and face us today, and which we have always admitted. But they were problems of development, not of depression; they were problems of advance, not of retreat.
I confess that a good many of these problems seem to me to have been discussed in the recent past by some members of the government in a way which indicated that they were rather not expecting to have the responsibility of solving them. They did, however, during those days and weeks and months make specific, categorical and confident statements that they would solve them, not at some vague and future date but quickly and decisively because the Prime Minister is a quick and decisive gentleman. It is in the light of these statements and the implementation of the promises that they contain that this government will be judged.
